prompt.context: After returning from a trade show, the CEO of a large grocery distribution center calls you. He enthusiastically describes a new technology which could be used to automate part of his company's process. He asks whether you think this would be a good idea for his business. Knowing that this CEO is a tech-enthusiast who loves innovation for the novelty of it, you ponder the implications.
prompt.question: How would you tackle this problem? Should the company automate part of its distribution process?

clarifying_info.q: Does the company have a specific financial goal or target for this decision?
clarifying_info.a: No specific goal. The CEO trusts us and will do whatever we advise. This is to test business judgment.

clarifying_info.q: How many shipments does the company make and to how many stores?
clarifying_info.a: Shipments are made to roughly 50 grocery stores in the immediate area, and the company does 1 million shipments per year.

clarifying_info.q: What are the costs to automate?
clarifying_info.a: Two components: (1) a one-time outlay of $4M, and (2) recurring overhead, training, and additional maintenance costs of $1.0M per year.

exhibits.title: Distribution Center Hours by Phase (Current State)
exhibits.shows: A diagram of the three phases of the distribution process — Receiving, Holding & Packing, and Shipping — with the number of hours per week required in each phase under the current (non-automated) process.

data.note: All units are hours per week

exhibits.title: Distribution Center Hours by Phase (Automated State)
exhibits.shows: A diagram of the same three distribution phases showing the projected hours per week required under the automated process.

framework: Revenues: Recognize this is primarily a cost issue — the company is not capacity-constrained and automation will not generate additional revenue
Costs — Existing: Fixed (rent, mortgage, leases, overhead, salaries) and Variable (hourly employees, repairs & maintenance, inventory holding, shipping)
Costs — Incremental One-time: Initial automation capex, initial training costs, downtime (none in this case), severance pay for terminated employees
Costs — Incremental Ongoing: Servicing, repairs, additional facility operating costs (energy, insurance, etc.)
Product: Assess changes to product quality (none) and ability to distribute additional product types (none)
Other: Potential future synergies (e.g., new technology interfacing with future tech) and impact on relationships with employees, grocers, and suppliers

questions.prompt: Visualize and describe the distribution process flow for a grocery distribution center.
questions.guidance: Candidate should independently conceptualize the three phases: (1) Receiving, (2) Holding & Picking, (3) Shipping. If they do not, prompt them to do so before proceeding.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the total number of employees required in each function and the annual labor cost under the current process.
questions.guidance: Candidate should request the hours-per-week data and employee wage rates, then calculate headcount and annualize at 52 weeks (not 50).

math.setup: Employees = Total Hours / 40 hrs per employee per week. Weekly cost = Total Hours x Cost per Hour. Annual cost = Weekly cost x 52.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the change in headcount and annual labor cost under the automated process, and determine annual labor savings.
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply same wage rates and 40-hr week to the new hours. Key insight: Receiving is unchanged; Holding & Packing drops significantly; Shipping increases. Net employee change is a reduction of 44 employees.

math.setup: Apply same wage rates (Receiving $12/hr, Holding & Packing $17/hr, Shipping $14/hr) and 40-hr workweek to automated hours. Annualize at 52 weeks.
steps: Employee change: Receiving 0, Holding & Packing -119 (250-131), Shipping +75 (150-75) => net -44 employees
math.answer: Net reduction of 44 employees; annual labor savings of $2,015,000

questions.prompt: Calculate the break-even period for the automation investment.
questions.guidance: Candidate should net the annual labor savings against the incremental ongoing costs to get annual incremental contribution margin, then divide the one-time outlay by that figure. The break-even of ~3.9 years should be assessed for attractiveness in context of the CEO's motivations.

math.setup: Annual incremental CM = Annual savings - Annual incremental costs. Break-even = One-time outlay / Annual incremental CM.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the potential costs associated with each phase of the distribution process (Receiving, Holding & Picking, Shipping)?

categories.name: Labor
ideas: Severance pay if automating reduces headcount

categories.name: Technology & Training
ideas: Initial training for new automated systems

categories.name: Downtime & Transition
ideas: Cost of parallel running old and new processes

recommendation: The data suggests automation is financially viable: annual labor savings of $2.015M offset $1M in recurring incremental costs, yielding $1.015M in annual incremental contribution, against a $4M one-time outlay — a break-even of approximately 3.9 years

However, given that the CEO is motivated primarily by novelty rather than strategic necessity, the recommendation should weigh whether a ~4-year cash payback period is truly justified when the business is not facing capacity or cost pressure that demands immediate action
risks: Employee morale and relationship risk from reduction of ~44 positions
Technology risk: automation may increase shipping hours significantly, creating bottlenecks in that phase
The CEO's enthusiasm for innovation may lead to scope creep or over-investment beyond this initial project
If the technology becomes obsolete before break-even, the investment is stranded
next_steps: Conduct a detailed assessment of severance obligations and workforce transition plan
Validate the projected hour reductions in Exhibit 2 with a pilot or vendor reference
Evaluate whether the increase in shipping hours (3,000 to 6,000) creates capacity or quality risks
Review the company's cash position and opportunity cost of tying up $4M for ~4 years
